references.text: The men of Sodom were wicked and sinned greatly against the Lord, which is the background for the judgment the angels are now about to carry out.

The Lord says that the outcry from Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin very serious, and that He will go down to see if it is truly so. This is the direct reason why the angels are sent to destroy the city.
Abraham asks the Lord to spare the city if there are ten righteous people there, but there were not enough righteous ones to avert the judgment.
Fulfillment of the angels' words: The Lord rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, destroying the cities and the entire plain.
The destruction of the land is directly compared to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah with sulfur and salt – an image of God's judgment over persistent sin.
The prophet Isaiah says that if the Lord had not left a small remnant behind, Israel would have become like Sodom and Gomorrah – a parallel to total destruction.
Isaiah prophesies that Babylon will be as when God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, showing that the judgment on Sodom serves as a pattern for God's punishment.
Peter uses Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of God's judgment: He reduced the cities to ashes and made them an enduring warning to the ungodly in the future.
Both verses illustrate God's sovereign use of agents to carry out judgment on a specific place based on a direct command.
Identical theological theme with 2 Kings 18:25 regarding God's judgment carried out through an army claiming to act on the Lord's command.
Contrasting perspective: Jeremiah shows that judgment can be avoided through repentance, emphasizing that Sodom's fate in Genesis 19 occurred because this opportunity had passed.
Both texts link a city's downfall directly to the Lord's wrath against the people's sin.
Thematic parallel: Both texts describe destruction as a direct consequence of the Lord's judgment on a people.
Confirms the theology in Genesis 19:13 that God's judgment is a just response to the wickedness of the unrighteous.
Theological principle: Both texts show that complete annihilation is the consequence of despising the Lord's word and sinning against Him.
Thematic parallel: Both texts describe destruction as a divine act directed against human pride and sin.
Theological insight: Jeremiah 31:28 shows that the destruction in Genesis 19 is part of God's greater plan for justice and restoration.
Thematic parallel: Both texts describe God's vengeance upon a people who have done evil, either through angels or by urging the people forward.
Eschatological fulfillment: Revelation 11:18 shows that the principle in Genesis 19:13 (God destroys those who destroy) holds true in the end.
Thematic parallel: Both texts show that destruction is a direct consequence of God's command.
Theological principle: Both texts show that destruction is a consequence of not listening to God.
Eschatological fulfillment: Isaiah 24:3 shows that the principle in Genesis 19:13 (God's word leads to destruction) holds true in the end.
Thematic parallel: Both texts show that destruction is a direct consequence of God's command.
Thematic parallel: Both texts show that destruction is a direct consequence of God's wrath.
Thematic parallel: Both texts show that destruction is a direct consequence of God's wrath.
Thematic parallel: Both texts show that destruction is a direct consequence of God's judgment.
